comments.body: who owns this lifecycle? ie. if the background agent crashes or the server restarts, how do the background agents get restarted? i mean i know that there is the state preserved but who's making them durable?
comments.author: You

comments.body: The TaskRunner inside the server process owns the lifecycle. Durability comes from three pieces: (1) the task row in rho.sqlite (status, attempt count, heartbeat, session file) is the source of truth; (2) each task runs in its own pi session whose file is the resume checkpoint; (3) on every server start the runner recovers — tasks stuck in `running` are requeued with attempt+1 (or failed + user notified once attempts are exhausted), and finished tasks whose outcome message was never delivered are re-delivered. Nothing depends on the process surviving. This was exercised for real during the e2e: a dev-server restart mid-task resumed from the row and completed on attempt 2.

comments.body: Clarification: background_task is not a static global tool. Every incoming channel message builds its agent session with a fresh tool instance whose create-callback closes over that message's conversation key, channel id, and target. The model never passes routing information — it can't get it wrong — and the task row is created already knowing exactly which conversation and channel its outcome must be delivered to.

comments.body: Added both layered scenarios to the plan's validation section: a contacts app that must reuse the existing contacts table, then an events app that must create a new events schema while referencing contacts for invites. The shared-runtime direction is recorded in the plan too: move schema/migrations/generated client out of @rho/core (installed, non-modifiable) into a runtime-owned package living with the modifiable extension layer — one SQLite db for system + extension tables, system tables prefixed (e.g. _sys_). Today's `rho.db` handed to extensions from core is the stopgap until that package exists.
